They also published an essay written by him. In parts of the interview, Melnichenko repeated Kremlin talking points. He said that Ukraine is a battlefield between Russia and the West, and he thinks the West ignored Russia's security concerns and threatens its sovereignty. But then it got more interesting. Melnichenko did not call for Putin to go, but - and it's a big but - he argued for a change that would bring about an end to one-man rule in Russia. He said Russia needs to engage more with the world. Prokopenko thinks the tycoon was trying to stir a public conversation. It was a "call on rich people like him to start talking", she says. The journalist who interviewed him, Arkady Ostrovsky, tells me the pair had "tense and heated discussions" in "hotels and cafes, mostly drinking coffee, lots of coffee, sometimes smoking". He says the tycoon seemed to be "genuinely thinking" about his answers, rather than giving politician-style spin. Nothing in Russia is simple, and most observers think the interview probably happened with some form of approval - implicit or explicit - from the Kremlin. We don't know why authorities would have been happy to authorise the unusual call for change; it's possible they were trying to show that some degree of pluralism still exists in the country. No tycoons came out to support him. Still, the journalist feels that Melnichenko was not speaking for himself alone, but also for his fellow businessmen. Some of them are hoping that after Putin's departure, the country might become an "oligarchic republic", as journalist Ostrovsky puts it - something like how it looked in the 1990s, with the business elites in charge. Based on his years of reporting on Russia, Ostrovsky says that many of the country's mega-rich currently feel a "sense of complete dead end, which this war has led Russia to… [an] absence of the future". But even if the tycoons are thinking about the future, there's a slim prospect of them acting any time soon, it seems. Browder, the Putin critic, says that although many of them are unhappy, they're unlikely to conspire against Putin while he is still alive. "They understand that if they were to do anything that would challenge Putin, he would kill them. And Putin is a very paranoid little man." Mike Calvey, an American financier who used to be a key investor in Russia, agrees. "What can they do besides just go straight to the prison and lose their assets? It's easy for people who are sitting in London to say that, 'why don't you just all go stand up and go straight to prison?' That's really what would happen." news.titleTr: Mexican drug lord Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo dies age 80
news.summaryTr: Known as the 'Boss of Bosses', he was the head of all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel in the 1980s before his arrest broke up his drug organisation.
news.articleText: Mexican drug lord Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo dies age 80 - Published Notorious Mexican drug lord Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo has died in hospital aged 80. Félix Gallardo was widely considered one of the biggest drug smugglers in history and is credited with building an alliance between criminal groups in Colombia and his own Mexican cartel. Known as The Godfather or the 'Boss of Bosses', Félix Gallardo was the head of the all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel, which reigned over Mexican drug trafficking at the height of the cocaine boom of the 1980s. At the time, it created a new modus operandi in the illegal drug trade which endures to this day. He had been in state custody since 1989. The name Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo will echo through the annals of drug-trafficking history more than any other except perhaps Pablo Escobar's. He led the organisation which revolutionised drug smuggling in the region by entering into partnership with the Colombian cartels, particularly Escobar's Medellín Cartel, to combine production in the Andes with Mexican transportation across the border into the United States. At one point an estimated 80% of all cocaine that entered the US came from the Medellín Cartel. Félix Gallardo and his organisation played a major role in smuggling it in. At its height, the Guadalajara Cartel under Félix Gallardo influenced Mexican politics and law enforcement, controlling entire police networks and state governorships. In 1985, the net started to tighten around the leaders of the cartel following the torture and murder of a DEA agent, Enrique 'Kiki' Camarena. Camarena had angered them after he had discovered and then destroyed a vast marijuana plantation in Chihuahua, which belonged to the criminal group. His death sparked one of the biggest manhunts the US government has ever launched in North America. In 1989, Félix Gallardo was captured and sentenced to decades in prison. In ill health, he was placed under house arrest since 2022 and died in hospital in his native Guadalajara. In the 1980s, Joaquin 'El Chapo' Guzmán was introduced to Félix Gallardo, who put him in charge of handling logistics for his drug organisation. From the subsequent break-up of Félix Gallardo's organisation after his arrest, the Sinaloa Cartel emerged, led by Guzmán, now another man synonymous with large-scale drug trafficking. In 2019, Guzmán was sentenced to life in prison for charges including drug trafficking and money laundering following one of the most high-profile trials in recent US history. news.title: Jensen Huang weighs Nvidia comeback days after shock exit: FT

news.titleTr: Jensen Huang weighs Nvidia comeback days after shock exit: FT
news.summaryTr: Silicon Valley executives are reportedly organizing a campaign to bring Huang back and are looking to gain White House support.
news.articleText: Jensen Huang weighs Nvidia comeback days after shock exit: FT Silicon Valley executives are reportedly organizing a campaign to bring Huang back and are looking to gain White House support. Jensen Huang is reportedly considering a return as Nvidia CEO just days after resigning from the company following reports of affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a subordinate. Huang has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning to Nvidia, according to the Financial Times, citing multiple people familiar with the matter. One source told the FT they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for Nvidia’s chief’s return, and are looking to gain support from the White House. “Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” they said. Meanwhile, a public campaign called “Bring Jensen Back” has attracted more than 161,000 signatures, according to its organizers, who list Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney among its supporters. The campaign website also claims to have over 9,000 signatures from current and former Nvidia employees. The push for his return goes against calls for new leadership at the AI chipmaker and coincides with an independent board investigation and scrutiny of its chip sales to China. Related: Former Nvidia CEO Huang had third alleged affair: Reuters US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a “dramatic shake-up” of Nvidia’s leadership, urging the company to hire a CEO from outside the company, while US President Donald Trump suggested Thursday that former Apple CEO Tim Cook take the job. Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation following reports of alleged extramarital relationships, including one involving a woman whom US intelligence officials reportedly suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence. The controversy has also raised questions about Nvidia’s compliance with US restrictions on AI chip sales, particularly involving customers in Asia with potential ties to China. Nvidia shares fell as much as 14% on Thursday before recovering to close 4.3% lower, underscoring investor uncertainty over the AI chipmaker’s future leadership. Cointelegraph reached out to Nvidia for comment. Magazine: US sellers drive Bitcoin crash, Jensen plots comeback: Hodler’s Digest

news.articleText: US sellers drive Bitcoin crash, Jensen plots Nvidia comeback: Hodler’s Digest Anchorage Digital data suggests the Bitcoin selloff is being driven by US investors. A “war room” has been set up by supporters to reinstate Nvidia boss Jensen Huang. Bitcoin bottomed after the US midterm elections in 2018 and 2022 — and the great Bitcoin crash of November 2026 looks like history repeating. Bitcoin plunged more than $10,000 this week, and is currently trading at $65,116 for a 12.4% loss. According to Anchorage Digital researcher David Lawant, the call is coming from inside the house. “BTC sell pressure continues to come primarily from the U.S,” he noted, positing a chart highlighting showing continued heavy net taker sell flow primarily on Coinbase compared with overseas exchanges. The US spot Bitcoin ETFs have seen heavy outflows, losing $2.35 billion over the past two weeks, and influencer Axel Bitblaze noted that Bitcoin fell in the hour before the US open on all but two of the past fifteen days. Source: Anchorage Digital Binance founder Changpeng Zhao rebuffed the idea that Binance is behind the crash. “No, Binance did not sell crypto. I bought crypto in the past few days,” he said. He attributed the crash to money shifting to the Anthropic IPO, the Bitcoin ETF outflows, security fears about crypto in general in the wake of the Binance hack, and hot inflation data raising expectations of interest rate hikes. Markets are now pricing in a quarter point Fed hike in December. Bitcoin fell to a four month low near $62,000 on Sunday but has since rebounded above $65,000. The Crypto Fear and Greed Index fell to 10, which is Extreme Fear. History provides some good news in that Bitcoin more then doubled in price within 12 months of the 2018 and 2022 midterm elections. Jensen discusses Nvidia comeback days after resigning The Financial Times reports that Jensen Huang is plotting a comeback to the top job at Nvidia with allies, following a determined push in Silicon Valley to pressure the board to reinstate him. Nvidia shares plunged after Huang resigned as CEO and from the board on Nov. 12, with Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress named as interim CEO. The resignation came shortly after news broke he’d had two other affairs, including one with a subordinate. Multiple people confirmed Huang has been discussing the idea of returning with confidants, even though an independent probe by the board is examining allegations he was romantically involved with a Chinese spy who helped ferry chips to China. The FT reported one ally saying that supporters have put together a “war room” to reinstate him. “Everybody that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the source said. A petition to reinstate Huang has garnered more than 100,000 signatures, including 5,600 current Nvidia employees, along with SpaceX boss Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney. The turmoil at Nvidia has weighed heavily on AI stocks and risk assets like cryptocurrency and the story still has a long way to run, with Congressional moves to investigate the issue and three bills being advanced to tighten AI chip export restrictions to China. According to the New York Time, intelligence officials reportedly briefed President Trump about the allegations Alice Huang was a Chinese spy a year ago, but he did not take any action. Ethereum should become post-quantum in 2027: Ethlabs Ethereum research group Ethlabs is withdrawing its Quick Slots proposal from the forthcoming Hegotá upgrade, and has urged core developers to urgently prepare the network for quantum attacks by 2027. On Wednesday, the group outlined “pqai27,” a proposed roadmap that aims to protect Ethereum against threats from quantum computing and artificial intelligence. At Devcon, researcher Justin Drake said he hopes to complete the transition in 2028 while the published roadmap still targets December 2029. Strategy gets booted from MSCI indexes Index provider MSCI has confirmed Bitcoin treasury company Strategy will be removed from its global equity indexes, following months of debate over whether crypto treasury firms qualify as operating businesses. Japan’s Metaplanet and crypto treasury company Upexi are also marked for deletion, while Ether treasury firm Sharplink is on a watchlist. The changes take effect after market close on Nov. 30. “Index inclusion meant ordinary passive investors, like someone holding a global index fund in their pension, were getting leveraged Bitcoin exposure they never chose. MSCI just fixed that,” Ryan Kirkley, CEO of Global Settlement Network, told Cointelegraph. Strategy fell 6.49% on Thursday and are down by more than one quarter over the past month. Bitcoin ETFs shed $2.35B in 2 weeks, BlackRock’s losing streak hits 11 US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) recorded $2.35 billion in net outflows over two consecutive weeks, as redemptions reached more than $1 billion each week. According to Farside Investors data, spot Bitcoin ETFs shed $1.07 billion between from Monday to Friday, following $1.28 billion in outflows the previous week, the largest weekly redemptions since late June. Friday marked the seventh consecutive trading session of net withdrawals, with about $1.71 billion redeemed since Nov. 5 Winners and Losers At the end of the week, Bitcoin (BTC) is down 12.4% to trade at $65,116, Ethereum (ETH) is down 14.4% to trade at $1,822 and XRP (XRP) is down 13.3% to $0.96. The total market cap is at $2.2 trillion according to CoinMarketCap. Among the biggest 100 cryptocurrencies, the top three altcoin winners of the week are Kite (KITE) with a 35.5% gain, Pieverse (PIEVERSE) on 33.8%, and Midnight (CRV) on 28.7%. The top three altcoin losers of the week are Zcash (ZEC) which was down 25.4%, Uniswap (UNI) down 23.2% and Aero (AERO) down 23.1%. Prediction of the Week Bitcoin’s ‘best buying opportunity ever’ has arrived: Mark Moss Bitcoin Opportunity Fund co-founder Mark Moss says that with banks and ETFs widening access to Bitcoin he expects a new record high in 2027. Wall Street’s embrace of Bitcoin has created the “best buying opportunity ever,” he said. Top FUD of the Week Microsoft confirms global outage resolved, rules out cyberattack Microsoft managed to restore Microsoft 365 services after a massive global outage disrupted Outlook, Teams and other applications for more than 24 hours, reiterating that the disruption was not caused by a cyberattack. Microsoft said that the outage stemmed from a problem introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade that emerged after a recent network change. “This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents,” the company said. MegaETH parent cuts 20% of staff amid restructuring, AI push MEGA, the organization behind Ethereum layer-2 network MegaETH, has reduced its workforce by 20% following months of restructuring as it expands into artificial intelligence products. The layoffs come as MEGA shifts its focus toward developing products on the MegaETH network, including artificial intelligence services. The organization has committed $30 million to the initiative. Metaplanet swings to $170M loss as Bitcoin sale hits earnings Metaplanet swung to a $170 million net loss in the first nine months of 2026, hit by a decline in the value of its Bitcoin holdings and a loss on the sale of 10,000 coins to demonstrate its ability to raise cash. The Japanese company, the world’s second-largest publicly traded corporate Bitcoin (BTC) holder, posted a net loss of 27.16 billion yen (about $170 million), compared with a profit of 13.53 billion yen ($84.6 million) in the same period last year. A 19.17 billion yen ($119.8 million) loss on the Bitcoin sale and an 8.04 billion yen ($50.3 million) loss from a decline in the value of its Bitcoin holdings outweighed gains in the operating business. Top Magazine Features of the Week Are Alt-L1s over? Security, costs drive smaller chains to Ethereum L1 blockchains Zilliqa, Gnosis and Ronin join the Ethereum ecosystem as the costs of going it alone grow, and the security and liquidity advantages become too hard to resist. Paraguay bank collapse shows stablecoins can offer a lifeline... of sorts Ueno’s collapse exposed the fragility of digital banking in Paraguay, as customers scrambled for access to their money and stablecoins offered a lifeline. Should you leave Australia to avoid paying 47% tax on crypto gains? Some Australian crypto investors are moving overseas to avoid the huge CGT increase from July 2027. But there are also less drastic ways you can pay less tax.

news.summaryTr: ABD'de yaşayan 31 yaşındaki Carter Stevens, çöpe atılan eşyaları toplayıp temizleyerek internet üzerinden satışa sunuyor. Eylül 2025-Eylül 2026 döneminde yaklaşık 140 bin dolarlık satış yapan Stevens, bulduğu mobilyalardan elektronik eşyalara kadar pek çok ürünü gelir kapısına dönüştürdü.
news.articleText: Çöpten servet çıkardı: Bir yılda 140 bin dolarlık satış yaptı - ABD'de yaşayan 31 yaşındaki Carter Stevens, çöpe atılan eşyaları toplayıp temizleyerek internet üzerinden satışa sunuyor. - Eylül 2025-Eylül 2026 döneminde yaklaşık 140 bin dolarlık satış yapan Stevens, bulduğu mobilyalardan elektronik eşyalara kadar pek çok ürünü gelir kapısına dönüştürdü. ABD'nin Tennessee eyaletindeki Nashville kentinde yaşayan Carter Stevens, başkalarının çöp olarak gördüğü eşyalardan gelir elde ediyor. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Ofis parkları ve lüks konutların çevresindeki çöp konteynerlerini inceleyen 31 yaşındaki Stevens, kullanılabilir durumdaki ürünleri toplayarak temizliyor ve eBay ile Facebook Marketplace gibi platformlarda satışa çıkarıyor. CNBC Make It'in incelediği belgelere göre Stevens, Eylül 2025-Eylül 2026 arasında yaklaşık 140 bin dolarlık satış gerçekleştirdi. Mart 2024'te başladığı bu işte el yapımı İran halılarından üst segment ofis koltuklarına, elektronik eşyalardan samuray kılıçlarına kadar pek çok ürün bulduğunu söylüyor. Stevens, kargo masraflarını da çöplerden bulduğu malzemelerle azaltıyor. Karton kutu ve ambalaj bandı gibi gönderi malzemelerini zaman zaman konteynerlerden temin ettiğini belirten girişimci, bu ürünler için yaklaşık yüzde 90 oranında ödeme yapmadığını ifade ediyor. 190 ofis koltuğundan 27 bin 600 dolar kazandı Stevens'ın bugüne kadarki en büyük kazançlarından biri, bir ofis binasının yakınında bulduğu Steelcase marka koltuklar oldu. Yeni fiyatları 1.000 doların üzerinde olabilen bu koltuklardan 190 tanesini kamyoneti ve kendi yaptığı römorkuyla taşıdı. Koltukların büyük bölümünü toplu olarak Facebook Marketplace üzerinden satan Stevens, bu işlemden 17 bin dolar gelir elde etti. Kalan koltukların tek tek satışından da 10 bin 600 dolar kazandı. Ayda yaklaşık bir büyük parti ürün bulması halinde eşyaları depolayıp satışa hazırlayabildiğini söyleyen Stevens, özellikle şirketlerin küçülme veya ofislerini boşaltma süreçlerini takip ediyor. Daha önce bir binanın önünde atılmış 120 ayakta çalışma masası bulduğunu da anlatıyor. Lüks konutların çevresinde ise West Elm marka mobilyalar, iPad'ler, elektronik cihazlar ve çalışır durumdaki elektrikli aletlerle karşılaştığını belirtiyor. Stevens, evindeki mobilyaların neredeyse tamamının çöplerden topladığı eşyalardan oluştuğunu söylüyor. Borçtan ve bağımlılıktan yeni bir gelir kapısına Stevens'ın bu işe yönelmesinin arkasında zorlu bir dönem bulunuyor. Üniversite yıllarında reçeteli Adderall ilacına bağımlılık geliştirdiğini ve 2018'de eğitimini tamamlayamadan okuldan ayrıldığını anlatıyor. İş bulmakta zorlanan Stevens, başlangıçta ikinci el mağazalarından vintage kıyafetler alıp satarak para kazanmaya çalıştı. Ancak kazancını kontrol etmekte zorlandığını, zaman zaman uyuşturucuya ve lüks harcamalara yöneldiğini söylüyor. 2021'de rehabilitasyon sürecinden geçen Stevens, 2023'te kira ödeyemediği için önce bir depoda, ardından otomobilinde yaşadı. Hayatındaki bu dönüm noktasının ardından harcamalarını kontrol altına almaya çalıştı. Mart 2024'te bir benzin istasyonunun yanında bulduğu, iyi durumdaki bir çift Nike Air Force 1 ayakkabısını temizleyip 35 dolara satması ise çöp toplama işine yönelmesinde önemli bir adım oldu. Stevens, elde ettiği gelirin her yıl aynı seviyede olacağından emin değil. Kazancının önemli bölümünün birkaç büyük satıştan geldiğini ve işin öngörülebilir olmadığını kabul ediyor. Bu nedenle gelirini biriktirmeye çalışırken gayrimenkul toptan ticareti alanını da araştırıyor. Buna rağmen çöplerden değerli eşya bulma ihtimalinin kendisini heyecanlandırdığını söyleyen Stevens, iyi görünen bir çöp konteynerini inceleme fırsatını kolay kolay kaçırmayacağını belirtiyor.

ABD'nin Tennessee eyaletindeki Nashville kentinde yaşayan Carter Stevens, başkalarının çöp olarak gördüğü eşyalardan gelir elde ediyor. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Ofis parkları ve lüks konutların çevresindeki çöp konteynerlerini inceleyen 31 yaşındaki Stevens, kullanılabilir durumdaki ürünleri toplayarak temizliyor ve eBay ile Facebook Marketplace gibi platformlarda satışa çıkarıyor. CNBC Make It'in incelediği belgelere göre Stevens, Eylül 2025-Eylül 2026 arasında yaklaşık 140 bin dolarlık satış gerçekleştirdi. Mart 2024'te başladığı bu işte el yapımı İran halılarından üst segment ofis koltuklarına, elektronik eşyalardan samuray kılıçlarına kadar pek çok ürün bulduğunu söylüyor. Stevens, kargo masraflarını da çöplerden bulduğu malzemelerle azaltıyor. Karton kutu ve ambalaj bandı gibi gönderi malzemelerini zaman zaman konteynerlerden temin ettiğini belirten girişimci, bu ürünler için yaklaşık yüzde 90 oranında ödeme yapmadığını ifade ediyor. 190 ofis koltuğundan 27 bin 600 dolar kazandı Stevens'ın bugüne kadarki en büyük kazançlarından biri, bir ofis binasının yakınında bulduğu Steelcase marka koltuklar oldu. Yeni fiyatları 1.000 doların üzerinde olabilen bu koltuklardan 190 tanesini kamyoneti ve kendi yaptığı römorkuyla taşıdı. Koltukların büyük bölümünü toplu olarak Facebook Marketplace üzerinden satan Stevens, bu işlemden 17 bin dolar gelir elde etti. Kalan koltukların tek tek satışından da 10 bin 600 dolar kazandı. Ayda yaklaşık bir büyük parti ürün bulması halinde eşyaları depolayıp satışa hazırlayabildiğini söyleyen Stevens, özellikle şirketlerin küçülme veya ofislerini boşaltma süreçlerini takip ediyor. Daha önce bir binanın önünde atılmış 120 ayakta çalışma masası bulduğunu da anlatıyor. Lüks konutların çevresinde ise West Elm marka mobilyalar, iPad'ler, elektronik cihazlar ve çalışır durumdaki elektrikli aletlerle karşılaştığını belirtiyor. Stevens, evindeki mobilyaların neredeyse tamamının çöplerden topladığı eşyalardan oluştuğunu söylüyor. Borçtan ve bağımlılıktan yeni bir gelir kapısına Stevens'ın bu işe yönelmesinin arkasında zorlu bir dönem bulunuyor. Üniversite yıllarında reçeteli Adderall ilacına bağımlılık geliştirdiğini ve 2018'de eğitimini tamamlayamadan okuldan ayrıldığını anlatıyor. İş bulmakta zorlanan Stevens, başlangıçta ikinci el mağazalarından vintage kıyafetler alıp satarak para kazanmaya çalıştı. Ancak kazancını kontrol etmekte zorlandığını, zaman zaman uyuşturucuya ve lüks harcamalara yöneldiğini söylüyor. 2021'de rehabilitasyon sürecinden geçen Stevens, 2023'te kira ödeyemediği için önce bir depoda, ardından otomobilinde yaşadı. Hayatındaki bu dönüm noktasının ardından harcamalarını kontrol altına almaya çalıştı. Mart 2024'te bir benzin istasyonunun yanında bulduğu, iyi durumdaki bir çift Nike Air Force 1 ayakkabısını temizleyip 35 dolara satması ise çöp toplama işine yönelmesinde önemli bir adım oldu. Stevens, elde ettiği gelirin her yıl aynı seviyede olacağından emin değil. Kazancının önemli bölümünün birkaç büyük satıştan geldiğini ve işin öngörülebilir olmadığını kabul ediyor. Bu nedenle gelirini biriktirmeye çalışırken gayrimenkul toptan ticareti alanını da araştırıyor. Buna rağmen çöplerden değerli eşya bulma ihtimalinin kendisini heyecanlandırdığını söyleyen Stevens, iyi görünen bir çöp konteynerini inceleme fırsatını kolay kolay kaçırmayacağını belirtiyor.

news.summary: Ticaret Bakanlığı Reklam Kurulu, internet siteleri ve sosyal medyada fal, medyumluk ve büyü hizmetlerine yönelik tanıtımları mercek altına aldı. Tüketicilerin korku ve batıl inançlarını istismar ettiği belirlenen reklamların durdurulmasına karar verildi.
news.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
news.titleTr: Ticaret Bakanlığı'ndan fal ve büyü reklamlarına yasak
news.summaryTr: Ticaret Bakanlığı Reklam Kurulu, internet siteleri ve sosyal medyada fal, medyumluk ve büyü hizmetlerine yönelik tanıtımları mercek altına aldı. Tüketicilerin korku ve batıl inançlarını istismar ettiği belirlenen reklamların durdurulmasına karar verildi.
news.articleText: Ticaret Bakanlığı'ndan fal ve büyü reklamlarına yasak - Ticaret Bakanlığı Reklam Kurulu, internet siteleri ve sosyal medyada fal, medyumluk ve büyü hizmetlerine yönelik tanıtımları mercek altına aldı. - Tüketicilerin korku ve batıl inançlarını istismar ettiği belirlenen reklamların durdurulmasına karar verildi. Ticaret Bakanlığı, fal, medyumluk ve büyü hizmetlerine yönelik reklam ve tanıtımlara karşı harekete geçti. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Reklam Kurulu, internet siteleri ile Instagram ve Facebook üzerinden yapılan söz konusu tanıtımları inceleyerek mevzuata aykırı buldu. Ticaret Bakanlığı Basın ve Halkla İlişkiler Müşaviri Bekir Kaplan, sosyal medya hesabından yaptığı açıklamada, Reklam Kurulu'nun 2026/1564 sayılı dosya kapsamında yürüttüğü incelemenin sonuçlandığını bildirdi. Reklamlar mevzuata aykırı bulundu İnceleme sonucunda söz konusu tanıtımların tüketicileri yanıltıcı ve aldatıcı nitelikte olduğu tespit edildi. Reklamların, Ticari Reklam ve Haksız Ticari Uygulamalar Yönetmeliği'nin ilgili hükümleri ile 6502 sayılı Tüketicinin Korunması Hakkında Kanun'un 61'inci maddesine aykırı olduğu belirlendi. Bu kapsamda Reklam Kurulu, fal, medyumluk ve büyü hizmetlerine ilişkin reklamların durdurulmasına karar verdi. "Vatandaşların inançlarının istismarına izin vermeyeceğiz" Bekir Kaplan, vatandaşların korkularının, manevi duygularının ve batıl inançlarının ticari kazanç amacıyla kullanılmasına izin vermeyeceklerini vurguladı. Bakanlık, tüketicileri yanıltan ve hassasiyetlerini istismar eden tanıtımlara yönelik denetimlerin sürdürüleceği mesajını verdi. FAL, MEDYUM VE BÜYÜ TANITIMLARINA TİCARET BAKANLIĞI REKLAM KURULUNDAN DURDURMA KARARI! İnternet siteleri ve sosyal medya platformları üzerinden fal, medyumluk ve büyü hizmetlerinin tanıtımını yaparak vatandaşların korkularını ve batıl inançlarını istismar eden reklamlar mercek altına alındı. Reklam Kurulu, 2026/1564 sayılı dosya kapsamında yaptığı incelemede; internet sitesi, Instagram ve Facebook üzerinden gerçekleştirilen medyum, büyü ve fal tanıtımlarının tüketicileri yanıltıcı ve aldatıcı nitelik taşıdığına karar verdi. Söz konusu tanıtımların; - Ticari Reklam ve Haksız Ticari Uygulamalar Yönetmeliği’nin 5/1-g, 7/1, 7/2, 7/3, 7/4, 7/5, 9/1, 9/5, 27/3 ve 32/1’inci maddelerine, - 6502 sayılı Tüketicinin Korunması Hakkında Kanun’un 61’inci maddesine aykırı olduğu tespit edildi. Bu kapsamda, 6502 sayılı Kanun’un 63’üncü ve 77/12’nci maddeleri uyarınca söz konusu reklamların durdurulmasına karar verildi. Vatandaşlarımızın korku, maneviyat ve batıl inançlarını ticari kazanç amacıyla istismar eden tanıtımlara izin vermiyoruz. Ticaret Bakanlığı Basın ve Halk İlişkiler Müşavirliği @ticaret — Bekir Kaplan 🇹🇷 (@bekir_kaplan) November 14, 2026

news.title: 74 ülkeyi etkileyen Microsoft kesintisinin ekonomik bilançosu ortaya çıktı
news.summary: Microsoft, Outlook, Teams, OneDrive ve Copilot dahil birçok hizmeti etkileyen küresel kesintinin siber saldırıdan kaynaklanmadığını açıkladı. Şirket, teknik sorunun giderildiğini ve kalan kullanıcılar için hizmetlerin yeniden devreye alındığını bildirdi.
news.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
news.titleTr: 74 ülkeyi etkileyen Microsoft kesintisinin ekonomik bilançosu ortaya çıktı
news.summaryTr: Microsoft, Outlook, Teams, OneDrive ve Copilot dahil birçok hizmeti etkileyen küresel kesintinin siber saldırıdan kaynaklanmadığını açıkladı. Şirket, teknik sorunun giderildiğini ve kalan kullanıcılar için hizmetlerin yeniden devreye alındığını bildirdi.
news.articleText: 74 ülkeyi etkileyen Microsoft kesintisinin ekonomik bilançosu ortaya çıktı - Microsoft'un Outlook, Teams, OneDrive ve Copilot hizmetlerinde yaşanan küresel kesinti 74 ülke ve bölgeye yayıldı. - On milyonlarca kullanıcıyı etkileyen aksaklığın verimlilik kaybı kaynaklı ekonomik faturasının 7 milyar dolara ulaşabileceği tahmin ediliyor. Microsoft, cuma sabahı sosyal medya platformu X üzerinden yaptığı açıklamada müşterilerinden özür dileyerek kesintinin giderilmesine yönelik çalışmalarda gelinen noktayı paylaştı. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Şirket, geniş çaplı hizmet kesintisinin herhangi bir siber saldırıdan kaynaklanmadığını vurguladı. Açıklamada, "Bu, siber güvenlik veya yapay zeka kaynaklı olmayan teknik bir sorundu. Temel sorunu giderdik ve hizmetleri kalan müşteriler ile bölgelere yeniden ulaştırmak için çalışmalarımızı sürdürüyoruz." ifadelerine yer verildi. Kesinti 74 ülke ve bölgeye yayıldı Kesinti, kullanıcıların Outlook e-posta hizmeti, Teams, OneDrive ve yapay zeka asistanı Copilot'ta erişim sorunları bildirmesiyle gündeme gelmişti. Yaklaşık 24 saat süren aksaklığın ilk saatinde 74 ülke ve bölgeye yayıldığı belirtilmişti. CNN'in Anderson Economic Group'a dayandırdığı habere göre kesintinin on milyonlarca kullanıcıyı etkilediği ve verimlilik kaybı nedeniyle ekonomik maliyetinin 7 milyar dolara kadar çıkabileceği tahmin ediliyor. Microsoft, sorunun daha önce gerçekleştirilen ağ kapasitesi yükseltmesi sırasında ortaya çıktığını ve sonradan yapılan bir ağ değişikliğinin ardından etkisini gösterdiğini bildirmişti. Şirket, incelemenin tamamlanmasının ardından olayın nedenlerine ilişkin kapsamlı bir rapor yayımlayacağını duyurdu. Kesinti sonrası dolandırıcılık uyarısı Microsoft kesintinin siber saldırı olmadığını açıklasa da uzmanlar, yaşanan aksaklığın dolandırıcılar tarafından fırsata çevrilebileceği konusunda uyarıyor. Siber güvenlik şirketi Sophos'un tehdit araştırmacısı Aiden Sinnot, bu ölçekteki kesintilerin kullanıcılar arasında belirsizlik yarattığını ve kötü niyetli kişilerin bu ortamdan yararlanabileceğini belirtti. Sinnot, Microsoft'tan veya kesintiden etkilenen şirketlerden geliyormuş gibi görünen mesajlara karşı dikkatli olunması gerektiğini vurguladı. Özellikle bankalar ve mağazalardan geldiği iddia edilen acil işlem taleplerine, kişisel bilgi isteyen mesajlara ve e-posta ya da mesaj yoluyla gönderilen bağlantılara karşı temkinli olunması çağrısında bulundu. Şirketler için tek teknoloji sağlayıcısına bağımlılık uyarısı Küresel kesinti, şirketlerin iş süreçlerinde tek bir yazılım sağlayıcısına aşırı bağımlı olmasının yaratabileceği riskleri de gündeme getirdi. GlobalData sosyal medya analisti Smitarani Tripathy, e-posta ve ekip içi iletişim gibi temel uygulamalardaki kesintilerin kısa sürede şirketlerin tüm işleyişini aksatabileceğine dikkat çekti. Tripathy, tek bir teknoloji ekosistemine bağlı çalışan şirketler açısından hizmet güvenilirliğinin, alternatif iletişim kanallarının ve kesinti dönemlerinde zamanında yapılan bilgilendirmelerin iş sürekliliği için kritik önemde olduğunu belirtti. İş sürekliliği, şirketlerin beklenmedik kesinti, teknik arıza veya kriz durumlarında temel faaliyetlerini sürdürebilmesini sağlayan plan ve süreçleri ifade ediyor. Alternatif sistemlerin ve iletişim kanallarının önceden hazırlanması, bu tür aksaklıkların etkisini azaltabiliyor.

Özellikle bankalar ve mağazalardan geldiği iddia edilen acil işlem taleplerine, kişisel bilgi isteyen mesajlara ve e-posta ya da mesaj yoluyla gönderilen bağlantılara karşı temkinli olunması çağrısında bulundu. Şirketler için tek teknoloji sağlayıcısına bağımlılık uyarısı Küresel kesinti, şirketlerin iş süreçlerinde tek bir yazılım sağlayıcısına aşırı bağımlı olmasının yaratabileceği riskleri de gündeme getirdi. GlobalData sosyal medya analisti Smitarani Tripathy, e-posta ve ekip içi iletişim gibi temel uygulamalardaki kesintilerin kısa sürede şirketlerin tüm işleyişini aksatabileceğine dikkat çekti. Tripathy, tek bir teknoloji ekosistemine bağlı çalışan şirketler açısından hizmet güvenilirliğinin, alternatif iletişim kanallarının ve kesinti dönemlerinde zamanında yapılan bilgilendirmelerin iş sürekliliği için kritik önemde olduğunu belirtti. İş sürekliliği, şirketlerin beklenmedik kesinti, teknik arıza veya kriz durumlarında temel faaliyetlerini sürdürebilmesini sağlayan plan ve süreçleri ifade ediyor. Alternatif sistemlerin ve iletişim kanallarının önceden hazırlanması, bu tür aksaklıkların etkisini azaltabiliyor.

news.articleText: Futbolun yıldızı bu kez kamera karşısında: Ronaldo'dan Hollywood hamlesi - Futbol kariyerinin yanı sıra iş dünyasındaki yatırımlarıyla da öne çıkan Cristiano Ronaldo, televizyon sektörüne giriyor. - Portekizli yıldız, "Day 1s" adlı spor temalı dizinin yapımcılığını üstlenirken projede oyuncu olarak da kamera karşısına geçecek. Dünyaca ünlü futbolcu Cristiano Ronaldo, kariyerinde yeni bir sayfa açmaya hazırlanıyor. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Portekizli yıldız, Hollywood yapımı bir televizyon projesiyle eğlence sektörüne adım atıyor. Ronaldo'nun ilk dizi projesi olan "Day 1s"in spor kültürünü konu alacağı ve genç sporcuların başarıya ulaşma mücadelesini ekrana taşıyacağı belirtildi. Ronaldo, projede yalnızca yapımcı olarak görev almayacak, aynı zamanda oyuncu olarak da dizide rol üstlenecek. Futbol sahalarının yıldız isminin kamera karşısına geçecek olması, projenin dikkat çeken ayrıntıları arasında yer alıyor. Genç sporcuların mücadelesini anlatacak "Day 1s" adlı dizi, profesyonel spor dünyasına adım atmaya çalışan genç sporcuların hikayelerine odaklanacak. Yapımda sporcuların hedeflerine ulaşma çabaları, rekabetin yarattığı baskı ve takım arkadaşları arasındaki dostluk ilişkileri işlenecek. Dizinin futbol sahnelerinde gerçekçi bir anlatım hedeflendiği, senaryo çalışmalarında ise Hollywood'dan deneyimli yazarların yer aldığı ifade ediliyor. Ronaldo kamera karşısına da geçecek Sportscape Magazine'de yer alan habere göre yapımcılık görevini üstlenecek Ronaldo, dizide kendisine özel bir rolle oyunculuk da yapacak. Futbol kariyerinde kazandığı deneyimleri projeye yansıtması beklenen yıldız futbolcunun, genç oyuncularla birlikte kamera karşısına geçeceği belirtiliyor. Ronaldo'nun televizyon sektörüne adım atması, futbol kariyerinin ardından eğlence dünyasında da faaliyet göstermeye yönelik yeni bir girişim olarak değerlendiriliyor. Cristiano Ronaldo, futbol kariyerinin yanı sıra CR7 markası altında moda, otelcilik ve farklı ticari alanlarda yatırımlar yürütüyor. "Day 1s" projesi, yıldız futbolcunun iş dünyasındaki faaliyetlerini eğlence sektörüne taşıma adımlarından biri olacak.

news.title: Türkiye'den sonra NATO zirvesine ev sahipliği yapacak ülke belli oldu
news.summary: NATO, 2026'da Türkiye'de düzenlenecek zirvenin ardından liderlerin Arnavutluk'ta bir araya geleceğini açıkladı. Zirvenin tarihi henüz netleşmezken, Arnavutluk Başbakanı Edi Rama toplantının 2028'de yapılabileceğine işaret etti.
news.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
news.titleTr: Türkiye'den sonra NATO zirvesine ev sahipliği yapacak ülke belli oldu
news.summaryTr: NATO, 2026'da Türkiye'de düzenlenecek zirvenin ardından liderlerin Arnavutluk'ta bir araya geleceğini açıkladı. Zirvenin tarihi henüz netleşmezken, Arnavutluk Başbakanı Edi Rama toplantının 2028'de yapılabileceğine işaret etti.
news.articleText: Türkiye'den sonra NATO zirvesine ev sahipliği yapacak ülke belli oldu - NATO, 2026'da Türkiye'de düzenlenecek zirvenin ardından liderlerin Arnavutluk'ta bir araya geleceğini açıkladı. - Zirvenin tarihi henüz netleşmezken, Arnavutluk Başbakanı Edi Rama toplantının 2028'de yapılabileceğine işaret etti. NATO'nun bir sonraki liderler zirvesinin adresi belli oldu. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle İttifak, 2026 yılında Türkiye'de gerçekleştirilecek toplantının ardından liderlerin Arnavutluk'ta bir araya geleceğini duyurdu. Ancak zirvenin hangi tarihte düzenleneceği henüz açıklanmadı. NATO yetkilisi, uluslararası basında zirvelerin ve toplantıların sıklığının azaltılacağına ilişkin haberler üzerine Anadolu Ajansı'na yaptığı yazılı açıklamada, "Bir sonraki NATO Zirvesi Arnavutluk'ta düzenlenecek, ancak zirvenin tarihi henüz belirlenmedi." ifadelerini kullandı. Arnavutluk Başbakanı Edi Rama da zirvenin başkent Tiran'da yapılabileceğini belirterek toplantının 2027 yerine 2028'de düzenlenebileceğine işaret etti. NATO zirvelerinin sıklığı değişebilir 25 Haziran 2025'te Lahey'de gerçekleştirilen NATO Zirvesi'nin sonuç bildirisinde, 2026'da Türkiye'de yapılacak toplantının ardından liderlerin Arnavutluk'ta buluşma kararı aldığı belirtilmiş, ancak tarih paylaşılmamıştı. NATO'nun resmi açıklamasına göre zirveler, İttifakın siyasi ve güvenlik ihtiyaçları doğrultusunda Kuzey Atlantik Konseyi'nin kararıyla düzenleniyor. Son 10 yılda, Covid-19 kısıtlamalarının uygulandığı 2020 yılı dışında NATO liderleri her yıl farklı müttefik ülkelerin başkentlerinde bir araya geldi. Diplomatik kaynaklar ise ABD yönetiminin NATO liderler zirvelerinin her yıl yapılması uygulamasının sona erdirilmesini ve toplantıların iki yılda bir düzenlenmesini istediğini belirtiyor. İttifak içinde bu yönde girişimlerin bulunduğu ifade ediliyor. NATO'nun en üst düzey siyasi karar organı Kuzey Atlantik Konseyi'dir. Liderler zirvelerinde müttefik ülkelerin devlet ve hükümet başkanları bir araya gelerek İttifakın güvenlik politikalarını ve ortak önceliklerini değerlendirir.

items.articleText: Australian MP who lost both legs in alleged car attack discharged from hospital - Published Australian politician Helen Haines, who lost both of her legs after police say she was deliberately run down with a car, has been discharged from hospital. The independent MP was struck outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on October 19, in an alleged attack which horrified Australia. Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official. He is yet to enter pleas. Haines, 65, has been discharged, the Alfred Hospital said on Monday, after four weeks and several surgeries which resulted in the amputation of her legs. Haines, known for supporting stronger climate action and helping establish a national anti-corruption commission, entered parliament in 2019 as the Member for Indi after working as a nurse and midwife. Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established. Nugent's father said he and his wife had been long-time friends of Haines, and Nugent's lawyer has said his client has mental health concerns. The incident sparked a reckoning in the country more broadly over the tone of public debate. Though a motive is still unclear, politicians, law enforcement, and experts have said heated public discourse is heightening the threat of political violence in the country. items.summaryTr: The Nvidia scandal has raised questions over whether advanced AI chips ended up in China, despite US restrictions.
items.articleText: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says - Published Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says. Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees. Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business. Megaspeed said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence". It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". But while Alice Huang is said to have stepped down from her role as Megaspeed director near the end of 2023, there were suspicions that she was still heavily involved in the firm's operations, according to Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS C4ADS said that Huang was still "practically in control" of Megaspeed even after she had handed over the reins of the firm. Huang - who is of no relation to Nvidia's former boss - had been investigated by Singapore authorities in February 2025 as part of the country's probe into Megaspeed and other companies. Also on Sunday, US Congressman John Moolenaar said that Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the Select Committee on China, which he chairs, as well as the House Foreign Affairs and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence. The committee heads had threatened to issue subpoenas to Huang if he did not comply with their requests to testify. Moolenaar told CBS, BBC's US partner, that none were ultimately issued. Huang's testimony is expected to take place behind close doors, with the dates still being finalised. "That's going to be a very important meeting to understand to what degree privileged information was accessed, and to what degree this potential alleged Chinese spy influenced Nvidia's philosophy and may have had an influence on some of our policies with respect to AI and export controls," the congressman told the Face The Nation programme. Separately, a group of tech leaders, including Space X's Elon Musk, have been trying to rally support to have Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO. A representative for Huang declined to comment on a report in the Financial Times Sunday suggesting that he was discussing a comeback to the firm he co-founded. The BBC understands that the likelihood of Huang being reinstated to lead Nvidia is very low while the company's internal investigations are ongoing. The move would also face scrutiny from Washington, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling for Nvidia to hire its next CEO from outside the company. On Friday, Bessent had blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips. Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process". The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals. Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips. Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang. Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced semiconductors to China. While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls. Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations. Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate". China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology. items.title: Clothing factories shut in Bangladesh as workers strike over pay
items.summary: Workers are striking over demands for a minimum wage of 30,000 taka (£182) a month.
items.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
items.titleTr: Clothing factories shut in Bangladesh as workers strike over pay
items.summaryTr: Workers are striking over demands for a minimum wage of 30,000 taka (£182) a month.
items.articleText: Clothing factories shut in Bangladesh as workers strike over pay - Published Dozens of factories in Bangladesh's main clothes-producing area have been shut by workers striking over a higher minimum wage. Nearly 150 sites across the country have been closed in the textile hubs of Savar, Ashulia and Gazipur this weekend. The garment industry is big business for Bangladesh, generating nearly $40bn (£30bn) in exports every year and making up 10% of the country's total GDP. Workers are striking over demands for a minimum wage of 30,000 taka (£182) a month. The minimum monthly wage in Bangladesh is currently 12,500 taka but employees say this is not enough to deal with the cost of living crisis. On Sunday morning workers massed on the Dhaka-Tangail highway in Gazipur to block the road. Traffic was stopped by the protests for about an hour before police stepped in. A "No Work No Pay" provision of labour laws allows owners to suspend operations and withhold wages when production is disrupted. Police Supt Mohammad Amjad Hossain told the BBC officers shut factories in the city after the workers walked out. He said 13 factories were closed on Saturday night and "sixteen factories were closed during the morning unrest". - Wage protests force hundreds of Bangladesh garment factories to close - Published3 November The garment industry in Bangladesh employs about four million workers making clothes for big brands including H&M, Primark and Zara. Bangladesh is the world's second largest exporter of ready- to-wear clothes after China and it is feared that the current unrest could have a knock-on effect for international buyers if it carries on for substantial amount of time. The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA) is calling for protection for factories. "BGMEA and BKMEA have questioned the justification of continuing to participate in wage board negotiations without any assurance that the factories will be protected," BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan said. "Garment factories that have been unable to continue production due to the ongoing unrest will remain indefinitely closed from tomorrow under... Bangladesh's labour law." But critics say workers are being sacrificed for factories to churn out products at competitive prices. Joly Talukder, the vice president of the Garment Workers Trade Union Centre, told BBC's Newshour that "workers have carried the costs for years" while factory owners and global retailers profit from their exploitation. "They are asking for a wage they can survive on. How can any person of conscience stand against such a basic human demand?" she said. On 1 November the government formed a minimum wage board to recommend a revised pay structure for workers. The board, chaired by a senior district judge, said at its first meeting it would finalise any recommendations by the end of November. Once it is put in place, the revised pay structure is expected to take effect from 1 December.

items.title: Black Friday and tax return scams - don't fall for these
items.summary: Tens of thousands of scams are reported to HMRC - so it has advice on how to spot a fake request and refund.
items.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
items.titleTr: Black Friday and tax return scams - don't fall for these
items.summaryTr: Tens of thousands of scams are reported to HMRC - so it has advice on how to spot a fake request and refund.
items.articleText: Black Friday and tax return scams - don't fall for these - Published This month's Black Friday and the tax return deadline at the end of January are both opportunities for fraudsters to scam you. That's because people are more likely to expect emails, texts and other correspondence at this time of year. Fraudsters will use the dates to impersonate genuine organisations and retailers by pushing victims towards fake websites to steal personal information. Here's how to spot a scam and how you can avoid being caught out. Is it really HMRC? Here's how to tell If you are self-employed or have more than one source of income you will need to file a tax return by the end of January. Fraudsters seize on this deadline to blitz people with messages that look like they are official and from the UK's tax authority, HMRC. Any such calls or messages should be ignored, but you can also check whether an email, external, text message, external or phone call, external claiming to be from HMRC is genuine. "Reporting scams helps us shut them down and protect others," adds Lucy Pike, HMRC's chief security officer. New figures from HMRC, shared with the BBC, show that it received 95,340 reports of suspected scams in the year to the end of October. There were 900 reports of one specific scam which used emails containing a malicious attachment which directed customers to a fake gov.uk webpage designed to steal personal and financial information. To avoid being caught out, HMRC says: - it never contacts people by email, text or phone to tell them they are due a refund or ask them to claim one - it never asks for personal or financial information by email or text message - it never leaves threatening voicemails about legal action or arrest Is it a real deal? Here's how to check In the run-up to Black Friday you may be looking around for discounts, but fraudsters will impersonate genuine retailers to steal personal details or take payment for a product that will never be delivered. Kirsty Adams, a fraud and scams expert at High Street bank Barclays, says make sure you pause before you buy. "When you're scrolling on the sofa and a countdown timer starts ticking, or a deal pops up in your feed from an account that looks just like a brand you trust, it's easy to get swept up and pay before you've had a chance to check. "No deal is worth rushing for. So take a moment before you buy." The bank also advises doing these four things: - Pause and check, rather than being blinded by a countdown timer - Pay safely using a credit or debit card via a trusted payment service, not a bank transfer to a stranger - Open an official website or app yourself rather than clicking on links in emails, ads or social posts - Talk to a friend, family or your bank if you think something does not feel right, and calling your bank straight away if you think you've been scammed Related topics - Published7 days ago - Published19 October

items.title: Russia's mega-rich are already imagining a future after Putin
items.summary: Some Russian tycoons are pining after a return to a 1990s system of oligarchy, when businessmen enjoyed power
items.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
items.titleTr: Russia's mega-rich are already imagining a future after Putin
items.summaryTr: Some Russian tycoons are pining after a return to a 1990s system of oligarchy, when businessmen enjoyed power
items.articleText: Hours after launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, Vladimir Putin gathered Russia's richest men in the Kremlin's cavernous Yekaterininsky Hall. More than three dozen of them sat huddled along a wall, wearing face masks because of the Covid pandemic. One Russian newspaper reporter described them as "pale and sleep-deprived". On entering, Putin sat down at the opposite side of the hall, creating a vast space between him and the businessmen. As usual, he was wearing no mask. Using his typically coded language, he said he expected them to support the war. "I would like to call on you to show understanding of what is going on," he said, "and work together with the government to find the tools which would support production, the economy, jobs." In the Kremlin-published video of the meeting, none of the invited billionaires said a word. That silence has become a feature of the Russian super-rich. Over the decades of Putin's rule, they have learnt that the price of piping up could be high. In 2003, oil magnate Mikhail Khodorkovsky, Russia's richest man at the time, who was funding a number of opposition groups, accused Putin of presiding over rampant corruption. He spent the next 10 years behind bars, convicted of tax evasion, fraud and embezzlement - a warning to other would-be critics. He denied the charges. And even if any of the tycoons objected to the war, they have tended to keep their thoughts to themselves. But even in that silence, there are murmurings: some members of Russia's once-mighty business elite seem to be imagining a Russia after Putin. They are wondering if, once the president has left office or died, the country might look more like it did in the 1990s, when the oligarchs enjoyed the fruits of power - or even if a healthier politics may take root. The journalist Arkady Ostrovsky, a prominent Kremlin-watcher at The Economist newspaper who recently spent hours interviewing one of Russia's richest men, says he feels that a "historic, political shift is happening" in terms of how the ultra-rich view the future of the country. Restless tycoons The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 gave birth to a new, powerful force on the domestic scene: people who took advantage of the end of communism and became extraordinarily rich, and then wanted to control politicians for their own benefit. They were dubbed "the oligarchs", from Ancient Greek for the "few who rule". They had money, which back then meant power. This era of the "wild 1990s" was when the so-called "new Russians" burst onto the scene. Huge state companies came up for grabs, and men with the right connections became millionaires - even billionaires - almost overnight. Corruption was rife, cronyism rampant, and contract killings frequent. But almost immediately after Putin was first elected as president in 2000, he subjugated the oligarchs. He had little interest in sharing power with anyone else. He could afford to stand up to the billionaires because Russia's economy was getting back on its feet, and the central government was getting stronger. Bill Browder, a financier who used to be the biggest foreign investor in Russia, and was banned from the country in 2005 after campaigning against corruption, says the Russian tycoons cowered and wilted in front of Putin - for example at the Davos economic forum, in the pre-war years when they were still welcomed there. "I can remember seeing oligarchs walking around like they own the place, the most arrogant and self-confident individuals. And then Putin showed up, and it was just remarkable to see how these supposedly alpha-male-on-steroids individuals turned into absolutely subordinate, almost desperate schoolchildren," he tells the BBC. Since the outbreak of war in 2022, the Kremlin has kept Russia's rich businessmen in line with a ruthless policy of carrot and stick. Critics of the war have seen their assets seized, while loyalists have been rewarded with lavish government war contracts: today there are more Russian billionaires than ever (155 in total, according to Forbes magazine). Their collective wealth has reached a new high of nearly $700bn (£525bn). But even for those tycoons who have stayed loyal and been rewarded, all of that money doesn't seem to be making them happy. Some are growing restless. Autocracy, oligarchy or democracy? Their billions do not go as far as they used to: domestically, they cannot buy much political influence. "They have no cards, they have no game," exiled politician and analyst Dmitry Nekrasov says. "They're rich because they've got something to do with Putin, not the other way round." And outside of Russia, they are ostracised because of the Western sanctions imposed on Russia after its full-scale invasion. "They're treated like low-level criminals. They can't fly their private jets. Their yachts can't park in all the best harbours in Europe. It must be very awful and humiliating for them," says Browder, the avowed Putin critic. And so, quietly, some of their minds are turning to what happens after Putin leaves the scene. That's what I'm told by well-placed analysts, who are immersed in the world of these tycoons. There's no immediate prospect of the president's departure, and there's no reason to think he's in bad health. But Putin, who turned 74 last month, has served in the Kremlin for a quarter of a century; people in Moscow know that his exit will come one day. When asked by Reuters last year if he intends to serve until 2036, when his constitutional term technically ends, Putin replied: "Only God knows if we have enough health." If Putin resigned or died in office, the prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, would take over. But Mishustin has not exhibited any presidential ambitions (that's probably a key reason he was appointed). That would create something of a power vacuum. In that scenario, Russia-watchers I have spoken with envisage a few potential scenarios. Some in the West, and no doubt within Russia, hope that democracy might flourish in a post-Putin Russia, with government led by the people, rather than by a new cadre of oligarchs or a single autocrat. But this seems like the least likely path, analysts say. Key democratic institutions have been eroded or destroyed over Putin's rule. "Russia is so used to violence, it has grown unaccustomed to standard democratic procedures," says Alexandra Prokopenko, an exiled Russian journalist and analyst. Another path is more autocracy. A different figure could replace Putin and continue his culture of repression. But Prokopenko thinks this wouldn't be another strongman dictatorship - at least not right away. These things take time, she says: at first, Putin's successor would be weaker than him, with fewer resources. And then there's the third option: tycoons re-assert their power and Russia returns to something resembling a 1990s-style system of oligarchy. Dmitry Nekrasov, a former Kremlin adviser and opposition politician who now lives in exile, says under this scenario, the country would be governed by a handful of powerful elite clans in alliance with business interests. This last option, of course, is the one that many tycoons want. "They'd like to return to a time when they were listened to, when they were not stripped of assets and when they understood the rules of the game," says Prokopenko, who has spent a lot of time speaking to Russia's richest people. Though their power has been seriously curtailed since the 1990s, it's still worth listening to the tycoons: given their immense wealth, it seems likely that sooner or later they will try to re-assert their political influence. Already, some are "trying to be friends with the right sort of security officials or ministers", says Nekrasov, the exiled politician. But he says any further steps are "too dangerous to take". He says the behaviour of the tycoons in coming years will depend in part on their finances. Those who have lots of liquid cash will be more confident to "play political games" and jockey for position, preparing for a post-Putin country. But those whose wealth is dependent on state contracts or government goodwill will feel too afraid, in case they lose everything, he says. Prokopenko says there's already been a shift in how the businessmen talk about Putin. They used to nickname him "Nachalnik" (which translates as "boss"), as well as "Perviy" ("first"), or by his initials "VV" - all nicknames that convey a degree of respect. Now they call him "Ded", with what Prokopenko calls "a pinch of contempt". "Ded" translates as "oldie" or "granddad" - a much less reverent name. Some rich Russians are pining after a "return of politics into people's lives", she says, with less repression, more open speech, and healthier competition between parties and politicians. But at the moment, she says, they are too afraid to make that happen due to Russia's stifling atmosphere. Prokopenko interviewed one tycoon who physically sat on his phone during the whole conversation, because he thought it would make digital eavesdropping more difficult for secret police. "I thought that it's an absolutely Stalinistic type of fear. It's absolutely irrational," she says. A bombshell interview An interesting clue for what tycoons might want from a post-Putin future came from Andrey Melnichenko, who is known as the world's fertiliser king and is currently Russia's eighth richest man. Earlier this year, he surprised observers by giving an interview to The Economist - a rare thing for a rich Russian to do, especially to a publication from a country the Kremlin considers unfriendly. They also published an essay written by him. In parts of the interview, Melnichenko repeated Kremlin talking points. He said that Ukraine is a battlefield between Russia and the West, and he thinks the West ignored Russia's security concerns and threatens its sovereignty. But then it got more interesting. Melnichenko did not call for Putin to go, but - and it's a big but - he argued for a change that would bring about an end to one-man rule in Russia. He said Russia needs to engage more with the world. Prokopenko thinks the tycoon was trying to stir a public conversation. It was a "call on rich people like him to start talking", she says. The journalist who interviewed him, Arkady Ostrovsky, tells me the pair had "tense and heated discussions" in "hotels and cafes, mostly drinking coffee, lots of coffee, sometimes smoking". He says the tycoon seemed to be "genuinely thinking" about his answers, rather than giving politician-style spin. Nothing in Russia is simple, and most observers think the interview probably happened with some form of approval - implicit or explicit - from the Kremlin. We don't know why authorities would have been happy to authorise the unusual call for change; it's possible they were trying to show that some degree of pluralism still exists in the country. No tycoons came out to support him. Still, the journalist feels that Melnichenko was not speaking for himself alone, but also for his fellow businessmen. Some of them are hoping that after Putin's departure, the country might become an "oligarchic republic", as journalist Ostrovsky puts it - something like how it looked in the 1990s, with the business elites in charge. Based on his years of reporting on Russia, Ostrovsky says that many of the country's mega-rich currently feel a "sense of complete dead end, which this war has led Russia to… [an] absence of the future". But even if the tycoons are thinking about the future, there's a slim prospect of them acting any time soon, it seems. Browder, the Putin critic, says that although many of them are unhappy, they're unlikely to conspire against Putin while he is still alive. "They understand that if they were to do anything that would challenge Putin, he would kill them. And Putin is a very paranoid little man." Mike Calvey, an American financier who used to be a key investor in Russia, agrees. "What can they do besides just go straight to the prison and lose their assets? It's easy for people who are sitting in London to say that, 'why don't you just all go stand up and go straight to prison?' That's really what would happen." items.articleTextTr: Hours after launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, Vladimir Putin gathered Russia's richest men in the Kremlin's cavernous Yekaterininsky Hall. More than three dozen of them sat huddled along a wall, wearing face masks because of the Covid pandemic. One Russian newspaper reporter described them as "pale and sleep-deprived". On entering, Putin sat down at the opposite side of the hall, creating a vast space between him and the businessmen. As usual, he was wearing no mask. Using his typically coded language, he said he expected them to support the war. "I would like to call on you to show understanding of what is going on," he said, "and work together with the government to find the tools which would support production, the economy, jobs." In the Kremlin-published video of the meeting, none of the invited billionaires said a word. That silence has become a feature of the Russian super-rich. Over the decades of Putin's rule, they have learnt that the price of piping up could be high. In 2003, oil magnate Mikhail Khodorkovsky, Russia's richest man at the time, who was funding a number of opposition groups, accused Putin of presiding over rampant corruption. He spent the next 10 years behind bars, convicted of tax evasion, fraud and embezzlement - a warning to other would-be critics. He denied the charges. And even if any of the tycoons objected to the war, they have tended to keep their thoughts to themselves. But even in that silence, there are murmurings: some members of Russia's once-mighty business elite seem to be imagining a Russia after Putin. They are wondering if, once the president has left office or died, the country might look more like it did in the 1990s, when the oligarchs enjoyed the fruits of power - or even if a healthier politics may take root. The journalist Arkady Ostrovsky, a prominent Kremlin-watcher at The Economist newspaper who recently spent hours interviewing one of Russia's richest men, says he feels that a "historic, political shift is happening" in terms of how the ultra-rich view the future of the country. Restless tycoons The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 gave birth to a new, powerful force on the domestic scene: people who took advantage of the end of communism and became extraordinarily rich, and then wanted to control politicians for their own benefit. They were dubbed "the oligarchs", from Ancient Greek for the "few who rule". They had money, which back then meant power. This era of the "wild 1990s" was when the so-called "new Russians" burst onto the scene. Huge state companies came up for grabs, and men with the right connections became millionaires - even billionaires - almost overnight. Corruption was rife, cronyism rampant, and contract killings frequent. But almost immediately after Putin was first elected as president in 2000, he subjugated the oligarchs. He had little interest in sharing power with anyone else. He could afford to stand up to the billionaires because Russia's economy was getting back on its feet, and the central government was getting stronger. Bill Browder, a financier who used to be the biggest foreign investor in Russia, and was banned from the country in 2005 after campaigning against corruption, says the Russian tycoons cowered and wilted in front of Putin - for example at the Davos economic forum, in the pre-war years when they were still welcomed there. "I can remember seeing oligarchs walking around like they own the place, the most arrogant and self-confident individuals. And then Putin showed up, and it was just remarkable to see how these supposedly alpha-male-on-steroids individuals turned into absolutely subordinate, almost desperate schoolchildren," he tells the BBC. Since the outbreak of war in 2022, the Kremlin has kept Russia's rich businessmen in line with a ruthless policy of carrot and stick. Critics of the war have seen their assets seized, while loyalists have been rewarded with lavish government war contracts: today there are more Russian billionaires than ever (155 in total, according to Forbes magazine). Their collective wealth has reached a new high of nearly $700bn (£525bn). But even for those tycoons who have stayed loyal and been rewarded, all of that money doesn't seem to be making them happy. Some are growing restless. Autocracy, oligarchy or democracy? Their billions do not go as far as they used to: domestically, they cannot buy much political influence. "They have no cards, they have no game," exiled politician and analyst Dmitry Nekrasov says. "They're rich because they've got something to do with Putin, not the other way round." And outside of Russia, they are ostracised because of the Western sanctions imposed on Russia after its full-scale invasion. "They're treated like low-level criminals. They can't fly their private jets. Their yachts can't park in all the best harbours in Europe. It must be very awful and humiliating for them," says Browder, the avowed Putin critic. And so, quietly, some of their minds are turning to what happens after Putin leaves the scene. That's what I'm told by well-placed analysts, who are immersed in the world of these tycoons. There's no immediate prospect of the president's departure, and there's no reason to think he's in bad health. But Putin, who turned 74 last month, has served in the Kremlin for a quarter of a century; people in Moscow know that his exit will come one day. When asked by Reuters last year if he intends to serve until 2036, when his constitutional term technically ends, Putin replied: "Only God knows if we have enough health." If Putin resigned or died in office, the prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, would take over. But Mishustin has not exhibited any presidential ambitions (that's probably a key reason he was appointed). That would create something of a power vacuum. In that scenario, Russia-watchers I have spoken with envisage a few potential scenarios. Some in the West, and no doubt within Russia, hope that democracy might flourish in a post-Putin Russia, with government led by the people, rather than by a new cadre of oligarchs or a single autocrat. But this seems like the least likely path, analysts say. Key democratic institutions have been eroded or destroyed over Putin's rule. "Russia is so used to violence, it has grown unaccustomed to standard democratic procedures," says Alexandra Prokopenko, an exiled Russian journalist and analyst. Another path is more autocracy. A different figure could replace Putin and continue his culture of repression. But Prokopenko thinks this wouldn't be another strongman dictatorship - at least not right away. These things take time, she says: at first, Putin's successor would be weaker than him, with fewer resources. And then there's the third option: tycoons re-assert their power and Russia returns to something resembling a 1990s-style system of oligarchy. Dmitry Nekrasov, a former Kremlin adviser and opposition politician who now lives in exile, says under this scenario, the country would be governed by a handful of powerful elite clans in alliance with business interests. This last option, of course, is the one that many tycoons want. "They'd like to return to a time when they were listened to, when they were not stripped of assets and when they understood the rules of the game," says Prokopenko, who has spent a lot of time speaking to Russia's richest people. Though their power has been seriously curtailed since the 1990s, it's still worth listening to the tycoons: given their immense wealth, it seems likely that sooner or later they will try to re-assert their political influence. Already, some are "trying to be friends with the right sort of security officials or ministers", says Nekrasov, the exiled politician. But he says any further steps are "too dangerous to take". He says the behaviour of the tycoons in coming years will depend in part on their finances. Those who have lots of liquid cash will be more confident to "play political games" and jockey for position, preparing for a post-Putin country. But those whose wealth is dependent on state contracts or government goodwill will feel too afraid, in case they lose everything, he says. Prokopenko says there's already been a shift in how the businessmen talk about Putin. They used to nickname him "Nachalnik" (which translates as "boss"), as well as "Perviy" ("first"), or by his initials "VV" - all nicknames that convey a degree of respect. Now they call him "Ded", with what Prokopenko calls "a pinch of contempt". "Ded" translates as "oldie" or "granddad" - a much less reverent name. Some rich Russians are pining after a "return of politics into people's lives", she says, with less repression, more open speech, and healthier competition between parties and politicians. But at the moment, she says, they are too afraid to make that happen due to Russia's stifling atmosphere. Prokopenko interviewed one tycoon who physically sat on his phone during the whole conversation, because he thought it would make digital eavesdropping more difficult for secret police. They also published an essay written by him. In parts of the interview, Melnichenko repeated Kremlin talking points. He said that Ukraine is a battlefield between Russia and the West, and he thinks the West ignored Russia's security concerns and threatens its sovereignty. But then it got more interesting. Melnichenko did not call for Putin to go, but - and it's a big but - he argued for a change that would bring about an end to one-man rule in Russia. items.summaryTr: Known as the 'Boss of Bosses', he was the head of all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel in the 1980s before his arrest broke up his drug organisation.
items.articleText: Mexican drug lord Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo dies age 80 - Published Notorious Mexican drug lord Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo has died in hospital aged 80. Félix Gallardo was widely considered one of the biggest drug smugglers in history and is credited with building an alliance between criminal groups in Colombia and his own Mexican cartel. Known as The Godfather or the 'Boss of Bosses', Félix Gallardo was the head of the all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel, which reigned over Mexican drug trafficking at the height of the cocaine boom of the 1980s. At the time, it created a new modus operandi in the illegal drug trade which endures to this day. He had been in state custody since 1989. The name Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo will echo through the annals of drug-trafficking history more than any other except perhaps Pablo Escobar's. He led the organisation which revolutionised drug smuggling in the region by entering into partnership with the Colombian cartels, particularly Escobar's Medellín Cartel, to combine production in the Andes with Mexican transportation across the border into the United States. At one point an estimated 80% of all cocaine that entered the US came from the Medellín Cartel. Félix Gallardo and his organisation played a major role in smuggling it in. At its height, the Guadalajara Cartel under Félix Gallardo influenced Mexican politics and law enforcement, controlling entire police networks and state governorships. In 1985, the net started to tighten around the leaders of the cartel following the torture and murder of a DEA agent, Enrique 'Kiki' Camarena. Camarena had angered them after he had discovered and then destroyed a vast marijuana plantation in Chihuahua, which belonged to the criminal group. His death sparked one of the biggest manhunts the US government has ever launched in North America. In 1989, Félix Gallardo was captured and sentenced to decades in prison. In ill health, he was placed under house arrest since 2022 and died in hospital in his native Guadalajara. In the 1980s, Joaquin 'El Chapo' Guzmán was introduced to Félix Gallardo, who put him in charge of handling logistics for his drug organisation. From the subsequent break-up of Félix Gallardo's organisation after his arrest, the Sinaloa Cartel emerged, led by Guzmán, now another man synonymous with large-scale drug trafficking. In 2019, Guzmán was sentenced to life in prison for charges including drug trafficking and money laundering following one of the most high-profile trials in recent US history. Related topics - Published24 October 2019

items.articleText: Jensen Huang weighs Nvidia comeback days after shock exit: FT Silicon Valley executives are reportedly organizing a campaign to bring Huang back and are looking to gain White House support. Jensen Huang is reportedly considering a return as Nvidia CEO just days after resigning from the company following reports of affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a subordinate. Huang has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning to Nvidia, according to the Financial Times, citing multiple people familiar with the matter. One source told the FT they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for Nvidia’s chief’s return, and are looking to gain support from the White House. “Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” they said. Meanwhile, a public campaign called “Bring Jensen Back” has attracted more than 161,000 signatures, according to its organizers, who list Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney among its supporters. The campaign website also claims to have over 9,000 signatures from current and former Nvidia employees. The push for his return goes against calls for new leadership at the AI chipmaker and coincides with an independent board investigation and scrutiny of its chip sales to China. Related: Former Nvidia CEO Huang had third alleged affair: Reuters US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a “dramatic shake-up” of Nvidia’s leadership, urging the company to hire a CEO from outside the company, while US President Donald Trump suggested Thursday that former Apple CEO Tim Cook take the job. Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation following reports of alleged extramarital relationships, including one involving a woman whom US intelligence officials reportedly suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence. The controversy has also raised questions about Nvidia’s compliance with US restrictions on AI chip sales, particularly involving customers in Asia with potential ties to China. Nvidia shares fell as much as 14% on Thursday before recovering to close 4.3% lower, underscoring investor uncertainty over the AI chipmaker’s future leadership. Cointelegraph reached out to Nvidia for comment. Magazine: US sellers drive Bitcoin crash, Jensen plots comeback: Hodler’s Digest

items.articleText: US sellers drive Bitcoin crash, Jensen plots Nvidia comeback: Hodler’s Digest Anchorage Digital data suggests the Bitcoin selloff is being driven by US investors. A “war room” has been set up by supporters to reinstate Nvidia boss Jensen Huang. Bitcoin bottomed after the US midterm elections in 2018 and 2022 — and the great Bitcoin crash of November 2026 looks like history repeating. Bitcoin plunged more than $10,000 this week, and is currently trading at $65,116 for a 12.4% loss. According to Anchorage Digital researcher David Lawant, the call is coming from inside the house. “BTC sell pressure continues to come primarily from the U.S,” he noted, positing a chart highlighting showing continued heavy net taker sell flow primarily on Coinbase compared with overseas exchanges. The US spot Bitcoin ETFs have seen heavy outflows, losing $2.35 billion over the past two weeks, and influencer Axel Bitblaze noted that Bitcoin fell in the hour before the US open on all but two of the past fifteen days. Source: Anchorage Digital Binance founder Changpeng Zhao rebuffed the idea that Binance is behind the crash. “No, Binance did not sell crypto. I bought crypto in the past few days,” he said.
